clue.text: For example, very old packed theatre

indicators.note: packed means the word for 'for example' is filled with the other letters

parts.note: say, as in 'take say three apples'

explanation.surface: An ancient example of a theatre that was full to the rafters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Savoy is a famous London theatre on the Strand, home of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas.
explanation.definitionFit: The Savoy is a well-known London playhouse, so it is an example of a theatre.

clue.text: Gateleg G Plan table laden with natural produce

indicators.note: laden with means the phrase carries the answer inside it as a load

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A furniture description: a G Plan gateleg table loaded with fresh fruit and vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: G Plan is a British furniture brand; a gateleg table has swinging legs that support folding leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: An aubergine is a vegetable grown on a plant, so it counts as natural produce from the garden.

clue.text: Wear diamonds deposited in a Scottish bank

indicators.note: deposited in means the diamonds' letter is placed inside the bank

parts.note: a brae is a Scottish word for a hillside or riverbank
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: Someone wears jewellery that was lodged in a Scottish bank's vault.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a financial bank, but a brae is a hillside slope in Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear something down by rubbing or friction is to erode or scrape it away gradually.

clue.text: Starts to speak King's English with a slight twist

indicators.note: starts to means only the opening letter of each following word is used

explanation.surface: Advice to talk the King's English but with a slight affected accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A skew is a slant or bias, a small departure from straightness.

clue.text: One picks up scent of fish Ernest gutted

parts.note: a bass is a fish

indicators.note: gutted means the inside of the name is removed, leaving only its ends

explanation.surface: A cook smells a fish that a man named Ernest has cleaned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scent of fish' looks like one idea, but the definition stops at 'scent'.
explanation.definitionFit: A basset is a short-legged hound bred to follow trails by smell.

clue.text: Press disrupted routine, holding Prime Minister up

indicators.note: holding means the rearranged letters wrap around the reversed pair
disrupted means the letters of routine are thrown into a new order
in a down clue, up means the letters are read bottom to top, so backwards

explanation.surface: The newspapers upset the daily schedule, keeping the Prime Minister waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like journalists, but it is the verb meaning to urge.
explanation.definitionFit: To importune someone is to pester or urge them persistently, as when you press them for a favour.

clue.text: Bloke putting out large cigar crashed light goods vehicle

indicators.note: crashed means the combined letters are smashed into a new order
putting out means a letter is expelled from the word bloke

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A man stubbing out a big cigar crashed a small delivery vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing L from BLOKE leaves BOKE; with CIGAR these letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A cargo bike is a pedal bicycle with a load box, used to deliver small parcels.

clue.text: Crazy times packing a gun?

indicators.note: packing means the multiplication word holds the weapon inside it

parts.note: by means times, as in 'three by four'
an arm is a weapon, such as a gun

explanation.surface: Asking whether these mad times call for carrying a firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is British slang for mad or foolish.

clue.text: Daughter (minx!) left last bit of guacamole dip

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child, like a minx

indicators.note: last bit of means just the final letter of guacamole is used

explanation.surface: A cheeky daughter has left only the last scrap of the guacamole dip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dip' looks like part of the snack, but it is the definition: a small hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: A dimple is a small hollow or depression, for example in the cheek.

clue.text: Bringing back a bear found around Lima is fair game

indicators.note: found around means the reversed letters surround the Lima letter
bringing back means the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: Pooh is the bear of A. A. Milne's stories
Lima is L in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone brings back a bear spotted near Lima, Peru, as a fair catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair game' sounds like legitimate prey, but it means a game at a funfair. Hoopla is the fairground game of throwing rings over prizes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoopla is a sideshow at a funfair where players toss rings to win prizes.

clue.text: At the border, board wagon's sleeper accommodation

parts.note: a wain is an old word for a farm wagon
a cot is a small bed for someone sleeping

explanation.surface: Instructions to get on a train's sleeping carriage at a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' looks like getting on the wagon, but it is the wooden panelling along the lower part of a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Wainscot is wooden panelling fitted along the base of a room's walls, a border of boards.

clue.text: Never takes exercise in linen

indicators.note: takes means the dialect word holds the exercise letters within it

parts.note: nary is a dialect word meaning not one, never
PE is physical education, exercise at school

explanation.surface: Someone who never does any exercise while dressed in linen.
explanation.definitionFit: Napery is household table linen such as tablecloths and napkins.

clue.text: Long, ultimately dire boring thread

indicators.note: boring means the letter drills into the thread word

parts.note: yarn is spun thread

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of dire

explanation.surface: A long, dreadfully dull piece of thread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective describing the thread, but it is the verb meaning to desire.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to crave or desire it strongly.

clue.text: Small domestic animal that is nursing temperature

parts.note: a pet is a domestic animal

indicators.note: nursing means the words hold the temperature letter like a baby

parts.note: ie is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A tiny pet that is running a fever is being nursed.
explanation.definitionFit: Petite describes a person who is slight and dainty in build.

clue.text: Aga saga's hastily written sequel?

parts.note: an Aga is a range cooker that boils pots, and a quickly churned-out novel written just for money has the same name

explanation.walkthrough: An Aga saga is a genre of British novel about comfortable country life, named after the Aga range cooker. The Aga itself is a device that heats pots, which gives the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A potboiler is a novel produced quickly for money, the kind of hurried follow-up a popular writer might churn out.

clue.text: Oxygen trapped in intestine? This can be extremely painful

indicators.note: trapped in means the oxygen letter is held inside the intestine word

parts.note: the gut is the intestine
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: Trapped gas in the bowel can be agonising.
explanation.definitionFit: Gout is an inflammatory joint disease notorious for intense pain, especially in the big toe.

clue.text: Intense criticism — England's opener is a bit stuck on 99

parts.note: flak is heavy criticism

indicators.note: opener means the first letter of England's

explanation.surface: A cricket report: England's opening batsman, stuck on 99, faces harsh criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: A 99 is a British ice-cream cone with a stick of Flake chocolate pushed into it; the cricket surface hides this.
explanation.definitionFit: A Flake is the crumbly chocolate stick pushed into a 99 ice-cream cone.

clue.text: Travelled back after seeing opening of Fred Astaire's Top Hat

indicators.note: after seeing places the reversed travel word just after Fred's initial, so inside the pair of initials
opening of means the first letter of each word in the star's name, his initials
back means the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: rode means travelled on horseback or by vehicle

explanation.surface: A reference to the 1935 Fred Astaire film Top Hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening of' takes the initial of both names, and the reversed travel word comes after the F, so it sits between the two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A fedora is a felt hat worn on top of the head, so cheekily a 'top hat'.

clue.text: Wallop bird heading west

indicators.note: in an across clue heading west means read from right to left

parts.note: a knot is a wading bird

explanation.surface: A bird flying westwards gets hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonk is British slang for a hard hit, as in a big hit in cricket.

clue.text: Tomsk, eh? Unusually eastern name for a capital

indicators.note: unusually means the letters of Tomsk eh are in an odd order

explanation.surface: Someone surprised that Tomsk, a Siberian city, could be an Eastern capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The Smoke is an old nickname for London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Smoke is a traditional British nickname for London, from its once-sooty air.

clue.text: Followed orders of "Ottoman governor" (as found in dictionary)

indicators.note: as found in means the governor's title sits inside the dictionary letters

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
a bey was a governor in the Ottoman Empire

explanation.surface: Someone complied with the commands of an Ottoman official, according to the dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: To obey is to comply with or carry out instructions, so it matches following orders.

clue.text: Rabbit stuffing Loretta Young served up

indicators.note: served up says the hidden letters are read backwards
stuffing means the answer is the filling packed inside the actress's name

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Rabbit stuffing being served to the actress Loretta Young.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Rabbit stuffing' as the definition, but 'stuffing' is what signals the letters are inside Loretta Young; the definition is just 'Rabbit', British slang for chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: To rabbit, in British slang, is to talk on and on, which is to chatter or prattle.

clue.text: Brainless comments I ignored completely in French city

indicators.note: ignored completely means every I is dropped, not just one

parts.note: inanities are silly, brainless remarks
the letter I is removed every time it appears, three times in all

explanation.surface: Someone completely ignored foolish remarks in a city in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantes is a large city in western France on the Loire.

clue.text: Delicious drink reportedly quaffed on Capri occasionally

indicators.note: reportedly means the word is as it would be heard spoken

parts.note: necked is slang for drank quickly, quaffed

indicators.note: occasionally means only every other letter of Capri is used

explanation.surface: Something tasty was drunk on the island of Capri now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: NECKED said aloud sounds like NECT; then the alternate letters A and R of Capri.
explanation.definitionFit: Nectar was the drink of the gods, now used for any delicious beverage.

clue.text: He was into balloons; not once seen cycling

indicators.note: cycling means letters are moved from one end of the word to the other

parts.note: never means not once

explanation.surface: A balloon enthusiast who was never seen on a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: Jules Verne wrote Five Weeks in a Balloon, and Around the World in Eighty Days is associated with ballooning.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne, the French novelist, wrote Five Weeks in a Balloon, so he was keen on balloon travel.

clue.text: Saxon prince's most precious slivovic Tori Amos guzzled?

indicators.note: guzzled means the words have swallowed the answer whole

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: The singer Tori Amos drinking plum brandy as her most treasured thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Albert came from Saxe-Coburg, so he is the Saxon prince; Victoria was his beloved wife. Slivovic is a plum brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Victoria was the adored wife of Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha.

clue.text: Pain van Gogh's doctor uncovered

indicators.note: uncovered means the outer letters of the doctor's name are stripped off

parts.note: Dr Paul Gachet treated van Gogh and was painted by him

explanation.surface: Van Gogh's physician relieved his pain.
explanation.definitionFit: An ache is a dull continuous pain.

clue.text: Being more theatrical, runs about naked

indicators.note: naked means the word is stripped of its outer letters

parts.note: scampers means runs about playfully

explanation.surface: Someone feeling more dramatic runs about without clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naked' looks like a description of the runner, but it strips the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp means exaggeratedly theatrical or affected in manner; this is its comparative form.

clue.text: Cut. Bad cut

parts.note: a cut is an artificial channel or canal, and a channel for foul waste is a bad one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' suggests wounds and surgery, but a cut is also an old word for a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewer is an underground channel carrying waste water, a foul version of a canal.

clue.text: Watch out! His Majesty is dishing out a beating!

indicators.note: out means the letters of watch are put out of order

parts.note: a king is addressed as His Majesty

explanation.surface: A warning shout that the king is giving someone a thrashing.
explanation.definitionFit: Thwacking is hitting hard with a stick, so giving someone a beating.
